documentation: A range is a real value: a..b, a..<b, a until b, a downTo b and 'step' build a Lua list of the integers (floating-point ranges keep just their bounds), which works as an IntRange/LongRange/UIntRange/CharRange/... typed value. x in a..b compiles to plain comparisons. A Char is a one-character Lua string, so 'a'..'e' is the list of those strings.

declarations.name: rangeTo
declarations.documentation: a..b and a.rangeTo(b): the Lua list of the integers, or just the two bounds for a floating-point range

declarations.name: until
declarations.documentation: a until b and a.until(b)

declarations.name: downTo
declarations.documentation: a downTo b and a.downTo(b)

declarations.name: step
declarations.documentation: a..b step n, a downTo b step n and (a..b).step(n), as a for header or as a value

declarations.name: IntRange
declarations.documentation: Type annotation only: a range value is the Lua list of its integers (a floating-point range is a table of its two bounds). Printing a range value directly shows its elements, not 1..5

declarations.name: contains
declarations.documentation: x in a..b compiles to two comparisons; a stored range is a list, a floating-point range checks its bounds

declarations.name: CharProgression
declarations.documentation: 'a'..'z' is the list of one-character strings; also works as a for loop, in a when branch and with 'in'

declarations.name: CharRange
declarations.documentation: 'a'..'z' is the list of one-character strings; also works as a for loop, in a when branch and with 'in'

declarations.name: coerceAtMost

declarations.name: coerceIn
declarations.documentation: math.min(math.max(x, min), max); also accepts a closed range argument

declarations.documentation: range.first is the first element; range.first() works as on any list
